questions.stem: India is the world's LARGEST producer of:

options.option_text: Rice
Milk, pulses, jute, spices
Wheat (world rank 1)
Cotton

questions.explanation: India is #1 globally for MILK (since 1998, Operation Flood), PULSES, JUTE, mangoes, bananas, SPICES. Wheat/rice — India is #2 (after China). Cotton — India and China are both top producers, rank alternates.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The 'MILK COOPERATIVE' movement that made India the world's top milk producer is associated with:

options.option_text: Amul / Verghese Kurien / Anand, Gujarat
Mother Dairy alone
Karnataka Milk Federation
Government-run farms

questions.explanation: Amul — Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union (1946), Anand, Gujarat. Verghese Kurien ('Father of White Revolution') led Operation Flood from 1970. NDDB (National Dairy Development Board) formed to replicate model nationally. India overtook USA in 1998 as top milk producer.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The NATIONAL FOOD SECURITY ACT, 2013 provides subsidised food grains to:

options.option_text: Only APL households
Up to 67% of population (75% rural + 50% urban) at subsidised prices via PDS
All households
Only BPL

questions.explanation: NFSA 2013 — legal entitlement to 5 kg foodgrain/person/month at ₹3/kg (rice), ₹2/kg (wheat), ₹1/kg (coarse cereals). Covers ~81 crore people. Uses target PDS (TPDS). Priority Households + Antyodaya Anna Yojana categories. Pregnant women / children — maternity benefits (₹6000) + take-home rations.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: MSP (Minimum Support Price) is RECOMMENDED by:

options.option_text: Food Corporation of India (FCI)
Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)
NITI Aayog
RBI

questions.explanation: CACP — est. 1965 (originally APC), part of Ministry of Agriculture. Recommends MSPs for 22 mandated crops. Cabinet (CCEA) approves. FCI + state agencies do the procurement. Swaminathan Committee (2006) recommended MSP = 1.5 × cost (C2) formula; adopted in 2018.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The 'GREEN REVOLUTION' started in India in:

options.option_text: Early 1950s
Mid-1960s

questions.explanation: Green Revolution — India 1965-66 onwards. Led by M.S. Swaminathan (FAO's Norman Borlaug visited). HYV seeds (especially wheat, later rice) + fertilizers + irrigation. Dramatic wheat-output rise. Critics: monoculture, water table depletion in Punjab-Haryana, income gap from non-beneficiary regions.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Match each revolution with its FOCUS. A. Pink.  B. Silver.  C. Golden.  D. Round. List-II: 1. Onions / prawns.  2. Eggs / poultry.  3. Horticulture / apples / honey.  4. Potato.
questions.explanation: Revolutions by colour: Green (foodgrains), White (milk), Yellow (oilseeds), Blue (fisheries), Pink (onions/prawns), Silver (eggs/poultry), Golden (horticulture/apples/honey — 'honey revolution'), Red (meat), Round (potato), Grey (fertilisers), Black (petroleum), Evergreen (sustainable agri, 2nd Green revolution).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The SWAMINATHAN COMMITTEE (2004-06) famously recommended MSP based on:

options.option_text: Market prices only
Total cost of production (C2) + 50%
International wheat-futures prices
Historical 10-year averages

questions.explanation: Swaminathan Committee (NCF): MSP ≥ 1.5 × C2 (cost of production including imputed cost of family labour + rental value of owned land). Government (CACP) has adopted various formulas (A2+FL, C2) — 2018 Budget formally announced 1.5x A2+FL as MSP basis (farmers argued C2 is fairer). i.e., 1.5 × cost formula.
questions.subject: Economics

_fixes.was: Total cost of production (C2) + 50% — i.e., 1.5 × cost formula

questions.stem: Which agricultural fibre crop is called the 'Golden Fibre' of India and accounts for the bulk of jute-based exports originating from West Bengal?

options.option_text: Cotton, the dominant commercial crop of the Deccan plateau
Jute, the bio-degradable natural fibre crop of eastern India
Silk, the premium filament fibre from Karnataka sericulture
Hemp, the multi-purpose fibre crop of the Himalayan foothills

questions.explanation: Jute is called 'Golden Fibre' because of its golden sheen and high economic value; West Bengal produces over 75% of India's jute. Cotton is nicknamed 'White Gold' — confusing the two nicknames is the most common mistake examinees make on this question.

questions.stem: PM-KISAN (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi), launched in February 2019, provides direct income support to eligible landholding farmer families. What is the correct annual amount and disbursement pattern?

options.option_text: ₹4,000 per year, released in two equal instalments of ₹2,000
₹6,000 per year, released in three equal instalments of ₹2,000
₹8,000 per year, released in four equal instalments of ₹2,000
₹12,000 per year, released in six equal instalments of ₹2,000

questions.explanation: PM-KISAN provides ₹6,000/year via DBT in three instalments of ₹2,000 each (April–July, August–November, December–March). ₹4,000 and ₹8,000 are frequent wrong recalls; ₹12,000 confuses PM-KISAN with certain state-level top-up schemes.

questions.stem: The eNAM (electronic National Agriculture Market) platform was specifically designed to create a pan-India unified market for agricultural commodities by integrating which existing infrastructure?

options.option_text: FCI procurement centres and Central Warehousing Corporation depots
State-regulated APMC mandis under a common online trading portal
Primary Agricultural Credit Societies and cooperative bank branches
Gram Panchayat-level haats and rural periodic markets under PESA

questions.explanation: eNAM (launched April 2016) links APMC-regulated state mandis through a single online portal, enabling traders anywhere to bid on produce — removing fragmented state-level market barriers. FCI centres are for PDS procurement and storage, not competitive farmer-level price discovery, which is a common conflation.

questions.stem: The 'Price Deficiency Payment' model, piloted in Madhya Pradesh as 'Bhavantar Bhugtan Yojana', fundamentally differs from traditional MSP physical procurement because it?

options.option_text: Requires farmers to sell their produce only at FCI-designated centres
Transfers cash to bridge the gap between MSP and actual market sale price
Offers a storage bonus above MSP for depositing produce in public warehouses
Makes crop insurance mandatory before any MSP benefit can be disbursed

questions.explanation: Under Bhavantar, farmers sell freely at prevailing market prices and the state directly deposits the MSP-minus-market-price shortfall into their bank accounts, avoiding physical procurement costs. The storage-plus-advance model described in Option C is actually the Negotiable Warehouse Receipt mechanism — a different instrument under WDRA.

questions.stem: Which agricultural product received the FIRST Geographical Indication (GI) tag ever issued in India under the GI of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999?

options.option_text: Alphonso Mango from the Konkan coast of Maharashtra
Darjeeling Tea from the sub-Himalayan hills of West Bengal
Basmati Rice from the Indo-Gangetic agro-climatic zone
Nagpur Orange from the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra

questions.explanation: Darjeeling Tea holds GI Application No. 1, awarded in 2004–05, making it the first Indian product registered under the GI Act. Basmati Rice received GI recognition later, and Alphonso Mango's GI tag came years after Darjeeling Tea — candidates frequently guess Basmati due to its higher international profile.

questions.stem: The Warehousing Development and Regulatory Authority (WDRA), established under the Warehousing (Development and Regulation) Act 2007, primarily enables farmers to avoid distress post-harvest sales by allowing them to obtain bank credit against which instrument?

options.option_text: Kisan Credit Card linked to the crop loan disbursement system
Negotiable Warehouse Receipts backed by stored agricultural produce
Land ownership records registered under the DILRMP portal
Forward market contracts executed on NCDEX commodity exchanges

questions.explanation: WDRA-registered warehouses issue Negotiable Warehouse Receipts (NWRs) against stored commodities; banks treat NWRs as collateral for credit, letting farmers hold produce until prices improve instead of panic-selling. The KCC is a separate, broader credit instrument for farm operations — not a post-harvest storage pledge mechanism.

questions.stem: Under Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY), the farmer-payable premium for Kharif foodgrain and oilseed crops is capped at what percentage of the sum insured, with the remaining actuarial premium shared equally by the Centre and the state?

options.option_text: 1% of the sum insured, with the full balance borne by the Centre alone
1.5% of the sum insured, applicable uniformly to all notified crop types
2% of the sum insured, balance shared equally between Centre and state
5% of the sum insured, a uniform cap across all annual commercial crops

questions.explanation: PMFBY (2016) caps farmer premium at 2% for Kharif foodgrain/oilseed crops; the Centre and state each bear 50% of the remaining actuarial premium. 1.5% is the Rabi cap — the most tempting distractor — while 5% applies only to annual commercial/horticultural crops. A uniform '1% Centre-borne' option does not exist under the scheme.
